This module presents the Tanakh on its own terms. Here is how the Catholic Church speaks of the Jewish people — you can explore it or leave it.

The Second Vatican Council (Nostra Aetate 4) teaches that the Church is bound to the stock of Abraham by a spiritual bond, that she received the revelation of the Old Testament through the people of Israel, and that the Jews remain “most dear to God” for the sake of the fathers (cf. Romans 11:28–29). It decries every form of antisemitism.

Christians read the same Scriptures and find in them the One who said “Hear, O Israel” is the greatest commandment (Mark 12:29). The Church holds that God’s covenant with Israel has never been revoked (Catechism 839).

column4: Torah means teaching or instruction more than “law.” It is the covenant way of life given at Sinai — 613 commandments in the rabbinic count — received not as a burden but as a gift and a delight (Psalm 119).
The covenants with Noah, Abraham, Israel at Sinai and David form the spine of the Tanakh. A brit binds God and people in mutual faithfulness; God’s side is never withdrawn.
Chesed is steadfast covenant love — loyal kindness beyond what is owed. It is the quality God names first about Himself after Sinai (Exodus 34:6).
The seventh day is holy time — a sanctuary in time rather than space. It remembers creation and redemption from Egypt, and it is kept as a foretaste of the world to come.
Holiness means set apart for God. Israel is called a holy nation (Exodus 19:6), and the call “Ye shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy” (Leviticus 19:2) shapes all of daily life.
The anointed king from David’s line, hoped for in the Prophets — a figure of peace, justice and the ingathering of the exiles.
The four-letter Name (YHWH) is not pronounced; it is read as Adonai (“my Lord”) in prayer, or HaShem (“the Name”) in conversation. JPS prints it as LORD.
Exile is the great wound of the Tanakh and return its great hope — from Eden, from the land, and finally the ingathering promised by the Prophets.
